knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

```{r setup}
library(OncoCohortSelect)
```

Generalized pairwise comparisons (Buyse, 2010) compare two cohorts on several
endpoints ranked by clinical priority. This article describes the comparison
of pairs, the scoring rules for censored times, the statistics computed by
`WinStat()` and their confidence intervals.

## Pairs and priority

Every patient of one cohort (called the treatment cohort) is compared with
every patient of the other cohort (the control cohort). A pair is first
compared on the endpoint of highest priority. If this endpoint shows which
patient has the better outcome, the pair is a win or a loss for the treatment
patient; otherwise the pair is compared on the next endpoint, and a pair that
no endpoint decides is a tie. A binary endpoint decides a pair when the two
values differ. A time-to-event endpoint decides a pair when one time is known
to be longer than the other by at least a threshold; a threshold larger than
0 asks for a clinically relevant difference before a lower-priority endpoint
is consulted.

With $\pi_W$, $\pi_L$ and $\pi_T$ the proportions of pairs won, lost and tied,
the net treatment benefit, the win ratio and the win odds are

$$\mathrm{NTB} = \pi_W - \pi_L, \qquad \mathrm{WR} = \frac{\pi_W}{\pi_L},
\qquad \mathrm{WO} = \frac{\pi_W + \pi_T / 2}{\pi_L + \pi_T / 2}.$$

The net treatment benefit lies between -1 and 1 and is 0 when the cohorts do
not differ; the win ratio and the win odds are 1 in that case. The win ratio
ignores the ties, so it can be large when few pairs are decided.

## An example

One simulated trial with two cohorts of 50 patients, enrolled over 12 months
and analyzed at month 18, so that many survival times are censored.

```{r}
arms <- list(
  Cohort1 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 6, orr = 0.30, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 15),
  Cohort2 = CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = 8, orr = 0.45, resp.cor = 0.4,
                                      death.prop = 0.15, os.median = 18))
d <- SimCohorts(nsim = 1, n = c(50, 50), arms = arms, ae.rate = c(0.20, 0.35),
                cutoff = 18, a.time = c(0, 12), seed = 2)
eps <- list(
  Endpoint("OS", "tte", time = "os_tte", event = "os_event"),
  Endpoint("PFS", "tte", time = "pfs_tte", event = "pfs_event"),
  Endpoint("ORR", "binary", var = "response"),
  Endpoint("AE", "binary", var = "ae", higher.better = FALSE))
w <- WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort2", control = "Cohort1")
w$estimate
w$by.endpoint
```

`by.endpoint` gives, for each priority level, the proportions of all pairs won
and lost at that level and the proportion still undecided after it. Of the
pairs, `r round(100 * w$by.endpoint$undecided[1])`% are not decided by OS:
the pairs in which the shorter observed time is censored.

## Scoring rules for censored times

With the rule of Gehan (1965), the default, a pair is decided on a
time-to-event endpoint only when the shorter observed time is an event, so
that the comparison is certain. Pairs in which the shorter time is censored are
passed to the next endpoint, which gives the lower-priority endpoints more
weight as censoring increases.

The rule of Péron et al. (2018) uses the Kaplan-Meier estimate of each cohort
to score these pairs. The true time of a censored patient is given the
distribution of the Kaplan-Meier estimate of its cohort beyond the censoring
time, and the pair is won with the probability that the treatment time is
longer by at least the threshold and lost with the probability that the
control time is longer. The Kaplan-Meier estimate is not defined after the
largest observed time of a cohort, so the probability beyond that time is
counted only when the comparison holds wherever the true time lies; the rest
of the pair goes to the next endpoint.

```{r}
wp <- WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort2", control = "Cohort1", scoring = "peron")
wp$by.endpoint
rbind(Gehan = w$estimate, Peron = wp$estimate)
```

With the Péron rule, OS leaves `r round(100 * wp$by.endpoint$undecided[1])`%
of the pairs undecided instead of `r round(100 * w$by.endpoint$undecided[1])`%.
The script `inst/validation/validate_winstat.R` compares the results of both
rules with those of the BuyseTest package.

## Thresholds and repeated endpoints

The priority order and the thresholds are given by `priority` and `threshold`,
one threshold per priority level (0 for binary endpoints). An endpoint can be
used more than once with decreasing thresholds: below, a pair is first
compared on OS with a threshold of 3 months, then on the adverse event, then
again on OS with a threshold of 0, and finally on response.

```{r}
w3 <- WinStat(d, eps, treatment = "Cohort2", control = "Cohort1",
              priority = c("OS", "AE", "OS", "ORR"), threshold = c(3, 0, 0, 0))
w3$by.endpoint
```

With the Gehan rule used here, a pair decided by OS with the threshold of 3
months is not compared again. With the Péron rule, the second use of OS adds,
for the pairs still undecided by the adverse event, the probability of a win
at the threshold of 0 minus the probability of a win at the threshold of 3
months, so that no part of a pair is counted twice.

## Standard errors and confidence intervals

The proportions of pairs won and lost are two-sample U-statistics. With
$W_{ij}$ the score of the pair of treatment patient $i$ and control patient
$j$ ($1$ for a win and $0$ otherwise, or a probability with the Péron rule),
$m$ and $n$ the cohort sizes and $\hat\pi_W$ the mean of the $W_{ij}$, the
variance of $\hat\pi_W$ is estimated from the first-order H-decomposition as

$$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\pi_W) = \frac{1}{m^2} \sum_{i = 1}^{m}
\Bigl(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} W_{ij} - \hat\pi_W\Bigr)^2 +
\frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{j = 1}^{n} \Bigl(\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i = 1}^{m} W_{ij} -
\hat\pi_W\Bigr)^2,$$

and likewise for the losses and the covariance of wins and losses (Bebu and
Lachin, 2016). The confidence interval of the net treatment benefit is computed
on the scale of $\mathrm{atanh}(\mathrm{NTB})$, which keeps it within
$(-1, 1)$, that of the win ratio on the log scale, and that of the win odds is
the interval of the net treatment benefit transformed by
$(1 + x) / (1 - x)$.

```{r}
w$ci
```

With the Péron rule the Kaplan-Meier estimates are treated as known, so the
standard errors are approximate and tend to be too small. Decision rules based
on the net treatment benefit, the win ratio or the win odds with thresholds
calibrated by simulation, as in *Evaluating decision rules by simulation*, do
not use the standard errors.

## References

Bebu, I. and Lachin, J. M. (2016). Large sample inference for a win ratio
analysis of a composite outcome based on prioritized components.
*Biostatistics*, 17, 178-187. https://doi.org/10.1093/biostatistics/kxv032

Buyse, M. (2010). Generalized pairwise comparisons of prioritized outcomes in
the two-sample problem. *Statistics in Medicine*, 29, 3245-3257.
https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.3923

Gehan, E. A. (1965). A generalized Wilcoxon test for comparing arbitrarily
singly-censored samples. *Biometrika*, 52, 203-223.
https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/52.1-2.203

Péron, J., Buyse, M., Ozenne, B., Roche, L. and Roy, P. (2018). An extension of
generalized pairwise comparisons for prioritized outcomes in the presence of
censoring. *Statistical Methods in Medical Research*, 27, 1230-1239.
https://doi.org/10.1177/0962280216658320
